cards.title: Iterate One Variable on a Proven Category
cards.summary: Enter large existing categories and change exactly one major variable to stay familiar-but-novel.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product or category to build in, or deciding how bold a repositioning should be
steps: Target well-established, easy-to-understand categories rather than inventing a category from scratch: you avoid driving consumer education for something wildly new.
Run the 'one iteration' rule: change exactly ONE major variable from the core product expectation (e.g., package shape OR benefit framing OR format).
Avoid changing two or three things at once — that pushes the product into 'too novel,' breaking consumer adoption.
Diagnose failed launches by counting changes: serial founder Eric Ryan says he fails more often from being too novel than too familiar.

For an underperforming pitch or launch, strip it to the single most convincing differentiator instead of stacking four; audiences drop multiple simultaneous changes the way they drop multiple thrown eggs.
caveats: Ryan applies this beyond consumer goods (even B2B), but notes he knows consumer better; treat cross-domain claims as his opinion.
One-variable discipline is a probability argument, not a guarantee.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Hunt for Cultural Shifts a Category Has Missed
cards.summary: The opportunity sits between a macro cultural shift and a stagnant category that hasn't absorbed it yet.
cards.use_when: Scanning a stuck or commoditized aisle for a repositioning opportunity
steps: Walk the retail aisle physically and look for a 'sea of sameness' — near-identical packaging, colors and claims.

Identify a cultural shift already visible in another category the target category has missed (Method: 'lifestyling of the home' plus health/sustainability; the home-care aisle still equated cleaning with poison).
Frame the business as the gap between that trend and where the category currently sits.
Ask whether the category has made something unnecessarily complicated, or takes itself too seriously — Ryan reads both as signals of insecurity hiding in the category.
Bring a childlike or playful angle into a self-serious category (gummy vitamins for adults, patterned bandages).
caveats: Ryan's read is that over-complication or self-seriousness signals insecurity — his interpretation, not a proven law.
The shift must already be visible elsewhere; you are connecting existing dots, not predicting a market.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Cross-Industry Theft to Create Creative Tension
cards.summary: Steal aesthetics and mechanics from far-away industries; the further apart the dots, the more powerful the idea.
cards.use_when: Generating distinct product, packaging or brand directions in a saturated category
steps: Steal from as far away as possible rather than copying competitors — from personal care into home care, or housewares into dish soap.
Ask the core question 'what if this, but for that?' to bridge two disparate domains.

Apply the mechanic to concrete cases: vase shapes became Method bottles; a Tokyo building's pillowed skin texture became a handwash design; a Norwegian camping-fuel bottle's shoulders became the original Method bottle.
Design everything as an object of desire, not a package — if a product is meant to sit on a counter, you look at it more than you use it.
Note that the strongest ideas pair two opposing concepts (eco + chic) to create creative tension, which Ryan argues deepens the experience and loyalty.
caveats: Distant combinations 'are not always going to work' — failure rate rises with novelty.
Ryan built the first Method bottle this way partly because a designer was unaffordable; theft-by-riffing suited the constraint.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Design for the Familiar-Novel Intersection
cards.summary: Land products at the intersection of familiar and novel: too familiar loses differentiation, too novel kills trial.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a concept is differentiated enough to matter yet easy enough to adopt
steps: Test the concept on two axes: if it's too familiar it lacks differentiation; if it's too novel it feels foreign and is harder to get someone to try.
Aim for enough familiarity to give consumers a jumping-off point and enough novelty to make it a new experience.
Use familiarity anchors consumers already trust — e.g., fiber as a benefit people already believe is good for them — and add novelty at the brand/product level.
Accept that finding the intersection is 'easy to say, hard to find' — it is the art of the process, so generate several candidate bridges rather than assuming the first works.
caveats: No numeric ratio of familiar to novel is given; it is a judgment call.
Consumer-education burden is the practical cost of drifting toward novel.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Simplify Instead of Demonstrating Sophistication
cards.summary: Best entrepreneurs simplify complex ideas; over-complication is often ego and weakens the pitch.
cards.use_when: Tightening a pitch, product story, or positioning that sounds impressive but isn't landing
steps: Assume the category or pitch has been made unnecessarily complicated; ask how to simplify it back for the consumer.

Cut to one convincing reason to switch, not a list. In one growth call, an AI company kept saying 'we're better' in many ways but could not name the single biggest one — they forgot to say how they're different.
Substitute a concrete scenario: 'for this person, here's the problem with your current tool, and here's how we do it instead.'
Watch for ego-driven complexity — Ryan sees founders overcomplicating to signal specialness or justify valuation.
Treat simplification as transferable: it helps consumers get it and teams execute it.
caveats: The AI-company example is an anecdote, not a measured result.
This is Ryan's opinion; some categories (technical B2B) may legitimately need more explanation.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Brand Naming Constraints: One Word, Four Letters
cards.summary: Start naming from a core feeling word tied to the product's goal, aiming for one word and four letters.
cards.use_when: Naming a new brand or product line
steps: Identify a 'jumping-off word' derived from the product's ultimate goal or feeling — 'technique' for cleaning pointed toward Method; 'friendly' for vitamins pointed toward Olly.
Run the naming search purely on that feeling rather than on descriptive or functional terms.
Treat the holy grail as one word, four letters, which tends to be short, memorable and ownable.
Check the name against the category's existing associations: a name evoking illness or bureaucracy (e.g., legacy fiber brand names) reinforces the outdated positioning you're trying to escape.
caveats: Four letters/one word is a target, not a requirement — Method is six letters.
No naming-availability or trademark process is described here.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Reimagine the Aisle as the Consumer's Experience
cards.summary: Walk the actual aisle and study shopper behavior to find the real pain the category ignores.
cards.use_when: Doing first-hand category research before defining a product concept
steps: Physically stand in the vitamin aisle (or equivalent) and watch shoppers — Ryan observed people visibly stressed trying to choose something healthy, asking strangers what magnesium is for.
Note the practical failures: hard to shop, uninspiring brands, poor packaging — this is the signal to dig.
Identify the big cultural shift the category missed (millennials treating health and wellness as a lifestyle pursuit, visible in how SoulCycle reframed fitness as almost spiritual).
Translate the shift into a design question: 'what would the Soul Cycle of vitamins look like?'
Design the product as a lifestyle object — a counter-worthy jar with the cap doubling as the logo — so it has intrinsic value and gets used.
caveats: Single-category observation is a source of hypotheses, not a validated finding.
Ryan's SoulCycle/wellness framing is his interpretation of millennial behavior.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Translate Benefits on Packaging, Not Features
cards.summary: Sell the outcome word ('sleep', 'beauty') instead of the ingredient name consumers can't decode.
cards.use_when: Writing product-page, packaging or shelf copy for a technical or unfamiliar product
steps: Observe the inference gap: legacy vitamins listed ingredients like vitamin D or melatonin, forcing shoppers to already know what each does.
Rewrite the label or page as the benefit — 'sleep' instead of melatonin, 'beauty' instead of biotin, 'immunity' instead of a nutrient name.
Pair benefit naming with unique blends positioned around the outcome, not the molecule.
Apply the same logic online: headline the job to be done, and let the ingredient detail live lower on the page for those who want to verify.
caveats: Regulatory rules for supplement claims vary by market and were not covered; verify before publishing benefit claims.
Benefit-first naming works best when the underlying benefit is already believed (e.g., fiber is good for you).
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Look at What Everybody Else Does and Do the Opposite
cards.summary: A single structural contrast — like everyone is round, so we go square — can be the whole differentiator.
cards.use_when: Designing packaging or page layout in a visually homogeneous category
steps: Survey the category's physical or visual conventions (in vitamins, every jar was round; in dish soap, every bottle looked alike).
Choose the simplest structural inversion: square jar with a white cap, or a bottle shape borrowed from another industry.
Make the contrast the icon — one 'single stroke that cuts through the noise' rather than many small differences.
Verify the contrast is the kind of change that can be defended and repeated consistently across range extensions.
Keep the rest familiar so the inversion reads as novel rather than confusing.
caveats: The source presents 'square' as an example of the one-variable rule, not a formula to copy literally.
A visual contrast is not sufficient on its own; Method and Olly also changed positioning and naming.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Run Trend Trips with a 24-Hour Make Cycle
cards.summary: Kick off a trend trip with macro trends, assign in-field scavenger hunts, and turn findings into presented concepts within 24 hours.
cards.use_when: Planning a trend or inspiration trip intended to produce sellable concepts, not a photo library
steps: Kick off with the big macro trends to ground the group before going into the field.
Hire someone on the ground for the region (Asia, Europe) and visit the most influential retail in that market.
Give everyone an assignment/scavenger hunt: by the 5pm happy hour, each person must bring multiple ideas they're excited about, then the group picks a few.
At dinner, call the brief in to the in-house creative team in San Francisco (their morning), who work on it all day and send it back at end of day.
Present near-polished concepts at breakfast — so you can sell in new products before the flight home.
caveats: The speed is deliberate: two weeks later the emotion and wow factor are gone, per the source.
Depends on having a creative team in a distant time zone and on-the-ground local support.
Trend trips commonly fail because attendees return to overflowing inboxes; the deadline structure is what prevents that.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Pitch Buyers to Improve, Not to Prove
cards.summary: Bring concepts to retailers asking for feedback, not approval — especially for early product direction.
cards.use_when: Preparing to show a concept to retail buyers or partners
steps: Shift the framing from 'I'm here to prove myself' to 'I'm here to improve myself.'
Do not ask buyers to choose A versus B; invite their reaction into the process.
Bring more than a slide: bring the concept as close to real as possible so the reaction is to the work, not the deck.
Use the same fast-turnaround discipline: showing up with near-finished concepts quickly is the wow factor, since emotion fades over weeks.
caveats: This is Ryan's practice, not a rule buyers expect; some buyers will still want a straight pitch.
Ryan built an unusually close early relationship with Target, which is not available to every brand.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Solve the Work in the Creative Before Research
cards.summary: Resolve concept direction by making it, then use qualitative feedback and retailer reaction to guide the choice.
cards.use_when: Choosing between two or three distinct concept directions
steps: Take the candidate directions and have a designer and creative team bring each fully to life before deciding.
Ask first which one you personally are most excited about — this is the energy test.
Share with friends and family: if they don't like it, why would anybody else?
Run 'consumer auditions' — qualitative focus groups — not to let consumers pick A versus B, but to hear feedback that guides your own decision.
Also put the concepts in front of retailers for their input.
Prepare to run two very different concepts (e.g., a blunt comedian-led version and an elevated beauty-style version) rather than splitting the difference.
caveats: Consumer auditions are qualitative guidance, not a vote or a validated preference test.
The energy/enthusiasm test is subjective and may mislead when founders are too close to the idea.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Use 'If It's Hard, It's Probably Wrong' as a Signal
cards.summary: Treat friction and lack of flow as diagnostic signals, though genuine breakthroughs can require an uphill phase first.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep pushing a concept or change direction
steps: Track energy flow: if working on something gives energy back, it's a sign it's right.
If you're 'pushing water uphill' for months with pain and no traction, treat that as a warning rather than a badge of effort.
Watch for the break point: once insight starts unlocking the next insight and the narrative comes together, momentum accelerates sharply.
Do not equate effort with value — Ryan warns against assuming a billion-dollar outcome requires visibly billion-dollar amounts of struggle.
Caveat the rule with Ryan's own experience: he pushed uphill for roughly six months on a current concept before it broke.
caveats: Ryan states this as a heuristic, not a law; the source itself describes a months-long uphill phase before a concept worked.
Energy-flow judgments are personal and can be rationalized either way.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Build as an Artisan Operator
cards.summary: Combine creative imagination with predictable operating discipline — supply chain, finance, controls — rather than choosing one.
cards.use_when: Building the team, culture or operating model for a consumer brand
steps: Adopt Ryan's 'artisan operator' philosophy: companies that both innovate imaginatively and run predictable businesses.
Invest deliberately in operating infrastructure — supply chain, finance, controls — alongside creative capability.
Note the scarcity Ryan cites: few companies do both well at scale (he names Apple and Nike).
Protect a small, agile make-focused team; Ryan argues builders and doers thrive in a state of make while managers 'just get in the way' (a deliberately provocative framing).
caveats: 'Managers get in the way' is Ryan's strong opinion, not an operating rule to adopt universally.
The Apple/Nike comparison is illustrative, not evidence of a required model.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx

cards.title: Treat Selling as Transfer of Emotion and Energy
cards.summary: Early retail wins came from persistence and contagious belief, not from buyers believing in the product first.
cards.use_when: Selling into independent retailers, distributors or any gatekeeper as an unknown brand
steps: Recognize the realistic window: showing up at 6am to a local grocery store manager gave roughly three minutes to pitch a new premium cleaning brand.
Accept that the buyer may never believe in the product — aim to get them to believe in you, and to believe you'll keep showing up until they say yes.
Find genuine love and energy for what you're building first, so the emotion is real and transferable.
Pair that with the serial-founder pattern Ryan describes: being top 20% at two unrelated things (design plus hustle) rather than top 1% at one.
Be willing to do sample handouts and repeat visits past the point most people quit.
caveats: This describes early-stage, founder-led selling into local accounts; it does not map directly to online acquisition.
Persistence can tip into sunk cost; the source pairs it with the energy-flow test.
cards.source_name: How I Start $1 Billion Companies from Boring Products.docx
